newsitem.title: USA: AmEx's Chenault tests the glass ceiling.
newsitem.headline: AmEx's Chenault tests the glass ceiling.

text.p: The naming of Kenneth Chenault, a 45-year-old black man, to the No. 2 position at American Express Co on Thursday drew attention to the dearth of African Americans in the most senior positions of the biggest U.S. corporations.

Alfred Edmond Jr, vice president and executive editor of the magazine Black Enterprise, estimated that only about 10 black Americans occupied the loftiest executive positions at the biggest companies. "Ten years ago you were hard pressed to name one or two," he said.

Other prominent black Americans in the upper ranks of the biggest companies include Richard Parsons, president of Time Warner Inc ; Richard Nanula, chief financial officer of Walt Disney Co ; and Barry Rand, executive vice president for operations at Xerox Corp.

Chenault and others were "testing how high the glass ceiling really is," Edmond said. But "the real barrier has yet to be broken," as there are still no black chief executives at the biggest multinational corporations, he said.
Chenault, as heir apparent to Harvey Golub, American Express's chairman and chief executive, could eventually be the one to break that barrier.
Edmond said the number of blacks in the top positions had grown and there was reason for "limited optimism" their ranks will expand further.

He said a chief concern was corporate downsizing had reduced the number of blacks in middle management ranks. Edmond said there were studies showing downsizing hurt blacks while other groups have actually had net gains.
